stem:
An agency head says: "Our new online booking system cut the average wait at our main office from 2 hours to 30 minutes. We should use the same system in our provincial offices, where clients also wait for hours."

Which of these is assumed?
choices: Every client in the provinces owns a computer.
Provincial clients now wait longer than 2 hours.
Clients in the provinces are able to book online.
Waiting times at the main office will keep falling.
answer: Clients in the provinces are able to book online.
hints: The head says a system that worked in one place will work in another. What must be true in the new place for the system to work there too?
Find the evidence (the system worked at the main office) and the conclusion (use it in the provinces). Then ask what the system needs from clients in order to work.

Negate each choice. Be careful with choices that say "every" or "longer": the argument may not need that much. The assumption is the choice whose opposite means the system could not work in the provinces.

solution.methodName: Negation test: deny it, and see if the argument falls apart

steps.action: Find the argument: the system cut waiting at the main office (evidence), so use it in the provinces (conclusion).
Spot the gap: an online booking system only helps if clients can book online. The head takes for granted that provincial clients can do this.
steps.why: When an argument says "it worked there, so it will work here," it assumes the new place is alike in the ways that matter.

steps.action: Negate it: "Clients in the provinces are not able to book online." Then the system cannot cut their waiting, and the argument falls apart.
Test the close rival: "Not every client in the provinces owns a computer." Clients can still book with a phone or at a help desk. The argument survives, so this choice asks for too much.
steps.why: An assumption is something the argument needs. A claim stronger than what is needed is not assumed.

steps.action: Check the rest. The head says provincial clients "also wait for hours," not more than 2 hours, and the system already cut a 2-hour wait. Future waits at the main office do not affect the plan for the provinces.
The assumption is: Clients in the provinces are able to book online.

trapNotes.Every client in the provinces owns a com: This is too strong. Clients could book with a phone or at a help desk. If some clients have no computer, the argument still works.
trapNotes.Provincial clients now wait longer than: The head only says provincial clients "also wait for hours." The system already cut a 2-hour wait at the main office, so the argument works even if provincial waits are no longer than 2 hours.
trapNotes.Waiting times at the main office will ke: This is about the main office's future, not the provinces. Negate it, and the reason for using the system in the provinces is unchanged.
